newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communist leader slams Moscow's Chechen deal.
newsitem.headline: Communist leader slams Moscow's Chechen deal.

text.p: The leader of Russia's Communist opposition on Sunday condemned the Kremlin's new accord with Chechen rebels, saying it spelled the break-up of the nation and he demanded a vote of no-confidence in the government.

Gennady Zyuganov told reporters he had formally asked for a a special session of the State Duma lower house to be convened possibly Thursday or Friday which he was sure would back his opposition to the deal.

Vladimir Zhirinovsky, whose ultranationalist Liberal Democratic Party is the third largest in the Duma behind the communists and Our Home is Russia pro-government party, called in an interview with Interfax news agency for parliament to prevent the "destruction of the Russian state".
The Duma, which is not due to sit again until December 4, has relatively little power to overturn government policy. It is involved in a bitter debate over the 1997 budget, however.

Zyuganov told Interfax the accord signed on Saturday by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Aslan Maskhadov, leader of the rebel government, was "unconstitutional and de jure marks the beginning of the break-up of Russia".

While insisting he wanted peace in Chechnya, Zyuganov accused President Boris Yeltsin's closest advisers of short-circuiting parliamentary review of the agreement and of failing to consult the interior and defence ministers, both of whom control troops to be withdrawn under the deal.
Yeltsin ordered the last two brigades of Russian troops out of the region before Chechen elections on January 27.
"What was signed was agreed with no one," Zyuganov told the news conference, saying he wanted the Justice Ministry to review the legality of the agreement.

"It was discussed nowhere expect perhaps in the close entourage of Mr Yeltsin, which has long failed to take account of Russia's interests and is pursuing the territorial destruction of our country," Zyuganov said.
The deal, which came after nearly two years of war, stops short of granting Chechnya the full independence separatist leaders say they want.
But it does foresee giving the region considerable autonomy.
Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in the July 3 presidential election, summoned an emergency meeting of leaders of his national-patriotic union coalition on Sunday morning.

He told Interfax the Constitutional Court and parliament should review the deal, which he said "smells of a Belovezh Mark 2", referring to the treaty signed by Yeltsin and other leaders in December 1991 which formally broke up the Soviet Union.
The communists want to recreate the union in some form.
Movladi Udugov, one of the main Chechen negotiators of the accord, dismissed Zyuganov's objections.
"It's no surprise," he told Reuters. "If the agreement hadn't been signed yesterday he would be objecting too."
